question: We hired temps to clear a backlog of customer complaints; the temps gave sloppy answers, which caused even more complaints. What pattern is this?
text:
This scenario is a classic example of the Fixes that Fail (or Fixes that Backfire) system archetype[1].
In system dynamics, the Fixes that Fail archetype describes a situation where an urgent problem symptom is tackled with a quick, short-term solution[1]. While the short-term fix may temporarily alleviate the symptom, it triggers unintended consequences that ultimately feed back into the system and make the original problem worse[1].
Here is how the feedback structure maps to your scenario:
Problem Symptom: A growing backlog of customer complaints[1].
Short-Term Fix: Hiring temporary workers to clear the backlog quickly[1].
Unintended Consequence: The temporary workers delivered sloppy, low-quality responses[1].
Reinforcing Loop: The poor responses frustrated customers further, triggering a new wave of complaints and expanding the backlog[1].
This dynamic often connects to the Shifting the Burden archetype as well[2]. In that pattern, relying repeatedly on a quick symptomatic fix (like temporary staffing) distracts from or defers investing in fundamental, long-term solutions—such as root-cause problem solving, process improvement, or proper training[2].

2.chunk:
Archetype #3: Shifting the burden
The “shifting the burden” archetype shows what happens when we address the symptoms of a problem with a quick-fix solution. This solution is easier and faster than creating an upstream solution to the problem, and we are often meeting a very real, urgent need for a student. However, the quick-fix to the symptoms may actually impede our ability to invest time and energy to the fundamental solution. This makes it even harder to apply a fundamental solution and even more tempting to rely on quick fixes. Thus, the problem cannot be completely solved.
